title: I'm Still Here: Black Dignity in a World Made for Whiteness
author: Austin Channing Brown
target_audience: Readers interested in anti-racism and racial justice
White allies and advocates seeking understanding of Black experiences
Students and educators in race, sociology, or cultural studies
Church and faith-based communities reflecting on racial inequity
core_themes: Black identity and dignity in a predominantly white society
Navigating white spaces as a Black woman
primary_purpose: To illuminate the lived realities of being Black in America, challenge the assumptions and biases maintained by white-dominated institutions, and advocate for dignity, justice, and equity for Black individuals.

structure_format.organization: Chronological and thematic essays recounting personal experiences and reflections
features: Engagement with faith, work, and community

key_concepts_lessons: Blackness is not a problem to be fixed; Black dignity is both inherent and necessary.
White spaces—whether churches, workplaces, or communities—often center white comfort at the expense of Black people.
Microaggressions and institutional racism have daily, cumulative impacts.
Authentic allyship requires self-reflection, active listening, risk, and relinquishing privilege.
Black voices and experiences need to be centered, not tokenized.
Faith can be both a source of pain and resilience for people of color.
notable_features: Memoir format blending personal anecdotes and social criticism
Discussion of intersection of race, gender, and faith
Calls to action for white readers and institutions
Short, vivid chapters for accessible and powerful reading
cultural_historical_context: Published in 2018, amid ongoing discussions on systemic racism, police brutality, and the Black Lives Matter movement. Written by an African American woman involved in ministry and nonprofit work, the book enters the field of contemporary anti-racist literature in the Trump-era United States.
reception_impact: Became a New York Times bestseller
Frequently recommended reading in anti-racist education and church groups
Praised for emotional honesty and accessible narrative
Often used as a catalyst for discussion in schools, book clubs, and faith-based organizations
Noted for challenging white readers while affirming Black dignity and experience
comparable_titles: Between the World and Me by Ta-Nehisi Coates
So You Want to Talk About Race by Ijeoma Oluo
The Color of Compromise by Jemar Tisby
The Cross and the Lynching Tree by James H. Cone
